Problems & solutions

How can I get enough protein if I don’t like shakes?

Explore ordinary food options that can fit breakfast, lunch, dinner and snacks.

By Nutrition.Fitness · 15 September 2026 · 4 min read

The short answer

You can get protein from ordinary meals without drinking shakes. Start with foods you enjoy, such as beans, lentils, eggs, fish, meat, tofu, yoghurt or suitable alternatives, and work them into your existing routine. A powder is an optional convenience. Before chasing a number, check whether the target fits your circumstances and whether you actually need to change what you eat.

You do not have to drink protein shakes to eat enough protein. You can build meals around food you already like. If you dislike the taste, texture or price of powders, that is a perfectly reasonable reason to leave them on the shelf.

The useful question is what your current meals provide, and whether that matches your needs. Owning a shaker is not an entry requirement for getting stronger.

Start with your meals, not somebody else's target

Protein needs vary with your circumstances, including activity and health. A number copied from a very muscular stranger's social feed is not an individual assessment. If you have a medical condition, a restricted diet or a prescribed eating plan, discuss changes with a registered dietitian or your clinician.

The NHS balanced-diet guide includes beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other protein foods alongside vegetables, starchy foods, dairy or alternatives and fats. Milk and yoghurt also contribute protein. This is a varied diet, rather than a requirement to make every item in the cupboard a high-protein version.

Look at an ordinary day without judging it. Which meals already contain foods from those groups? Where are you trying to make an awkward change? A breakfast you skip because the proposed shake makes you gag probably needs a different breakfast, not a more expensive blender.

Build from foods you would happily eat again

MealFood-based optionHow to make it practical
BreakfastEggs on toast with tomatoesKeep eggs and bread available; use a version you can cook on a workday.
Breakfast without cookingYoghurt or a suitable alternative, oats and fruitCheck the label because products differ; choose a texture you enjoy.
LunchBean and vegetable wrap, or a chicken sandwich with saladUse the same filling for more than one meal if that suits you.
DinnerLentil bolognese, tofu stir-fry or fish with potatoes and vegetablesAdapt an existing family meal rather than adding a separate cooking session.
Something portableA sandwich, yoghurt kept chilled, or a suitable ready-to-eat snackChoose for the facilities you actually have, including safe storage.

These are meal ideas, not a prescribed day of eating or a calculation of your requirements. Portions depend on appetite, the rest of your food and any individual advice. Use ingredients appropriate for your allergies and dietary needs.

If you need numbers, compare the portion you eat

A label might list protein per 100g while you eat a different amount. As an illustrative calculation, a food labelled 10g protein per 100g would supply 15g in a 150g portion: 10 multiplied by 1.5. Those figures demonstrate the arithmetic; they are not a claim about a particular yoghurt or a portion everyone should eat.

For a homemade dish, add the protein values of the ingredients you use, then divide by the number of portions made. Check whether a label describes the drained, cooked or uncooked food so the calculation matches it. You do not need to repeat this for every meal indefinitely. If counting becomes stressful, use familiar meal combinations instead and seek help with any concern about adequacy.

What if you eat a plant-based diet?

Choose several foods you enjoy rather than expecting one ingredient to do everything: tofu in a stir-fry, beans in a chilli or lentils in a sauce, for example. Check the actual product when buying meat or dairy alternatives. Similar packaging does not mean identical nutrition.

A completely plant-based diet also involves nutritional considerations beyond protein. If you are changing your whole diet, obtain appropriate advice rather than treating a protein total as proof that everything is covered.

When would a powder still make sense?

It may be convenient if you like it and it solves a specific problem, such as having an option you can prepare quickly. Compare its cost, ingredients, storage and enjoyment with an ordinary meal or snack. If food already works, there is no nutritional prize for adding a tub.

Nutrition.Fitness sells supplements, so we have a commercial interest here. Our answer remains that they are optional. You should be able to use a programme and meal-planning approach without buying our powders or flavour shots.

Choose two ideas from the recipe collection that fit meals you already eat. Try those before shopping for a supplement. What is the actual difficulty you want to solve: time, appetite, variety or knowing what to cook?
